title: Special reason and Category 1: 9.1.3 (general) vs 9.1.1 (protected-official offences only)
statement: 9.1.3 says that if a special reason exists the court may decline to impose imprisonment “in the case of a Category 1 offence”. Read in context (9.1.3 opens with the mandatory minimum provisions, and footnote 2005, attached to that sentence, confines declining imprisonment to the protected-official injury and driving offences and then requires a therapeutic order), it means a Category 1 offence that also carries a mandatory minimum; 9.1.1 likewise confines the Category 1 exception to offences that are also mandatory minimum offences against protected officials. The literal words of 9.1.3 are wider. A special reason is itself an exception that the mandatory minimum provisions provide (9.1.3, first sentence), so the conflict is real only for Category 1 offences that carry a mandatory minimum (ss 15A/15B where the victim is not a protected official, ss 77B, 79A). Handling: for those offences the app follows 9.1.1 and footnote 2005 and proposes only imprisonment without a CCO; any other disposition proposed on a special reason (a non-custodial disposition, or imprisonment combined with a CCO) is shown as unresolved (caution) rather than passed, and not as an error (audit.category_1_2 (d), audit.cco_limits (6), cat1.custodial_required). For a Category 1 offence with no mandatory minimum (e.g. murder, rape) no special reason exists, so a non-custodial disposition is an error on every reading.

refs.q: If a court finds that a ‘special reason’ exists, it may decline to impose a term of imprisonment (in the case of a Category 1 offence) or may impose a non-parole period below the statutory minimum (in the case of minimum non-parole period offences).

title: CCE value threshold: “$50,000 or more” vs a rolled-up transaction that “exceeds $50,000”
statement: A CCE offence involves property or benefits “valued at $50,000 or more”, but 9.4 says a rolled-up charge qualifies only if a constituent transaction “exceeds $50,000”, while 2.4.5 says, of rolled-up charges themselves, a transaction “of $50,000 or more”. A transaction of exactly $50,000 is treated differently by these statements; the app shows this caution and marks the point unresolved. For the maximum check, the app does not rely on the doubled CCE ceiling for a rolled-up count whose largest transaction is exactly $50,000: a sentence above the ordinary maximum but within the CCE ceiling is shown with this caution, not failed (audit.maximum_applicable (7)); a charge whose value exceeds $50,000 only because of the rolled-up value does not qualify. 27.5.1 states the rolled-up rule as “at least one transaction of $50,000 or more”, as 2.4.5 does.

title: Aggregate fines: 12.5 bars one where an offence “is a standard sentence offence” but gives no test

title: Youth detention maximum across occasions: the unexpired part or the whole earlier term?
statement: 10.1.1.3 says the maximum period of youth detention also operates as the maximum that may be achieved by cumulation of sentences on several occasions, and that if the offender is already undergoing youth detention, cumulation orders only operate to the point when the maximum is reached. It does not say whether the earlier sentence counts in full or only its unexpired part. Youth detention is presumed concurrent with any other uncompleted term, whenever imposed (10.1.1.3). title: Fines for offences whose life or 25-year maximum is printed without a penalty level
statement: 12.1 says fines cannot be imposed as an alternative or in addition to imprisonment for Level 1 (life imprisonment) offences, and that for Level 2 offences (punishable by 25 years’ imprisonment) a fine can only be imposed in addition to imprisonment. Some register rows print a maximum of life or 25 years without a level. The Manual does not say whether the Level 1 and Level 2 fine rules apply to those offences. 12.1 excepts a body corporate from the Level 2 rule (a fine may be an alternative “if the offender is a body corporate”), and 5.1.1 excludes life imprisonment from the general fine of 10 penalty units per month. Handling: a 25-year maximum without a level — a fine alone, or as an alternative to imprisonment, imposed on a natural person → caution, unresolved (audit.fine_rules); a body corporate → no caution. A life maximum without a level — no general fine is available in any case (5.1.1; fine.maximum), which the maximum check enforces; a fine the row itself prints → caution. Never an error on the ground of the missing level.

title: OHS offences, company in liquidation: specific deterrence “not automatically” reduced (31.5) v “little or no part” (31.7.2)
statement: 31.5 says liquidation does not automatically reduce the weight to be given to specific deterrence, because a company is controlled by directors who may operate in the industry in future. 31.7.2 says that the sentencing judge must ignore the fact that the company is in liquidation and that the fine will never be paid, and must consider the assets and financial prospects at the time of trading, and that specific deterrence will have little or no part to play. Handling (app policy): fix the fine on the company’s assets and prospects at the time of trading; give specific deterrence of the company little weight, but the need to deter those behind it (31.5) may still be weighed; never fail reasoning that takes either view; show this caution where the company is in liquidation.

title: Indefinite sentence test: 4.4 (“a serious offender”; “or any special circumstances”) v 8.7 (“an adult offender … convicted of a ‘serious offence’”; “and any special circumstances”)
statement: 4.4 describes the indefinite sentence power as allowing a court sentencing “a serious offender for a serious offence” to impose an indefinite term if satisfied to a high degree of probability that the offender is a serious danger to the community “because of their circumstances, the nature or gravity of the offending, or any special circumstances”. 8.7, which sets out the scheme, says that an adult offender convicted of a ‘serious offence’ by the Supreme or County Court may be sentenced to an indefinite term, and that the court must be satisfied to a high degree of probability that, at the time of sentencing, the offender poses a serious danger “because of their circumstances, the gravity of the offending, and any special circumstances”. The two passages differ in the class of offender and in the connective (“or” v “and”). Handling: the gate (indefinite.requirements) and the audit follow 8.7, the section that states the requirements; reasoning that relies on 4.4’s wording (a single one of the matters, or the “serious offender” class) → caution, never an error on this ground. title: Aggravated burglary and home invasion: an uncharged loaded firearm as “very significant” aggravation vs the uncharged-conduct rule
statement: 27.2.2.2 says uncharged post-entry conduct that could have been charged as a more serious offence should not aggravate, that such criminality cannot be taken into account adversely, and that the duty to consider all circumstances of the charged offence gives way to the principle that no one is punished for an uncharged offence — yet a loaded firearm carried during a home invasion has been held a “very significant aggravating feature” even where no firearm offence is charged, because it revealed premeditation, illuminated the intention at entry and greatly increased the danger of the entry. title: OHS offences: death or injury “only relevant” to show the risk (31.2) vs harm that “must” be taken into account (31.3.2.4, 31.6.1)
statement: 31.2 says the OHS scheme is risk-based, not outcome-based, and that death or injury “will only be relevant in so far as it demonstrates the degree of seriousness of the relevant threat”; 31.3.2.4 says the actual result is of “very limited relevance” to gravity and may only illuminate the risk. Yet 31.3.2.4 also says death or serious injury “may be a relevant sentencing consideration as an impact of the offence or an injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offence” (the Act ss 5(2)(daa), (db)), and 31.6.1 says a court “must take into account” such harm, including through victim impact statements. The Manual does not reconcile the two. Handling: measure gravity by the breach and the risk, using the outcome only to illuminate the existence, likelihood and potential gravity of the risk; take death or injury into account as an impact of the offence (s 5(2)(daa), (db)) only where causation is proved beyond reasonable doubt, and do not let the outcome stand in for the gravity of the breach; when comparing cases, compare the breaches, not the outcomes (31.1.3). Note that s 32 requires serious injury for that offence (fn 4667). Show this caution wherever death or injury occurred; never fail reasoning that treats proved harm as victim impact.

title: Firearm possession: criminal history and prohibited or FPO status listed as elevating or aggravating (33.2.1) vs the priors rule (6.3.1.2) and the element rule (5.2.8)
statement: 33.2.1 lists “an offender’s criminal history, especially any prior firearms convictions” among factors that “may elevate the seriousness” of a possession offence, and “the status of the offender either as a prohibited person or the subject of a firearm prohibition order, and the nature and extent of their prior criminal history” among factors that “may aggravate”; 33.1.3.1 says criminal history may warrant “a more substantial sentence”. But prior criminality “cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish an offender” (6.3.1.2), and a factor that is an element of the offence cannot be counted as aggravating (5.2.8). For s 5(1), s 5(2), s 5AB(2), s 5AB(3) and s 112B the prohibited-person or FPO status is an element, and that status often arises from a prior term of imprisonment (fn 4865). The Manual does not reconcile these. Handling: criminal history may be used for what it shows about the purpose of the possession and the risk (33.2.1.1), to limit mitigation, and in specific deterrence (33.3), but must not lift the sentence beyond what the offence warrants; where the status is an element of the charge, do not count it again as aggravating, though the reason for the prohibition (serious offending v “unrelated, minor offending”, 33.2.1.1) may inform gravity. title: Plea discount for “worst category” offending: competing authorities
statement: The Manual records competing lines of authority on whether a plea to worst-category offending earns a discount: one holds that the more serious the crime, the greater the weight of the plea; more recent authority asks whether the enormity of the criminality means the plea’s utilitarian benefit must yield to public protection and the rule of law. Elsewhere the Manual says that in all but exceptional cases the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction. For the worst murders a plea is now generally held to be a necessary condition for fixing a non-parole period, but it does not necessarily save the offender from life imprisonment. Handling: for worst-category offending assume neither an enlarged discount nor none; state which line is applied and show this caution.

title: Hardship to family or third parties: “exceptional circumstances” (7.6) vs the current Victorian test (7.6.4)
statement: 7.6 says the family/associates limb “demands” that the offender establish exceptional circumstances, and the first paragraph of 7.6.4 says the same. 7.6.4 then records that Victorian authority previously required “highly exceptional” circumstances; that the NSW no-exceptionality approach for Commonwealth offences “is now followed by the Victorian Court of Appeal” (the Manual does not say whether only for Commonwealth offences); and, hedged (“It appears now”), that for Victorian offences the hardship must rise above the general hardship of prisoners’ families and be “so significant that they will weigh heavily in the sentencing calculus”. Handling: require cogent evidence and hardship that rises above the general and weighs heavily; where mitigation rests on that test without a finding of “exceptional” circumstances, caution, not error; never mitigate for third-party hardship without cogent evidence.

refs.q: The second limb, hardship to the family (or other associates) of the offender, demands that the offender establish exceptional circumstances before it will go to mitigating sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

refs.q: Hardship to a third party as a consequence of imprisonment is not normally a mitigating circumstance. But a court has discretion to mitigate sentence when that sentence causes hardship to a third-party and it is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances.

refs.q: For Victorian offences, the Court of Appeal has previously said that hardship to third parties is only relevant in mitigation where it is ‘highly exceptional’ or ‘the exceptional case where the plea for mercy is seen as irresistible’.

title: Public opprobrium as punishment: expressly unclear
statement: The Manual says loss of reputation may be a form of punishment, but it is unclear whether opprobrium resulting from conviction may be considered. It notes the tension with an offender who held, or exploited, a position of privilege or power, and lists only a few instances held relevant: seriously or significantly damaging publicity causing hardship; and loss of career from the conviction (less arguable if the career was used to offend; possibly mitigating where the offending is remote from the employment). Handling: give opprobrium weight only within the listed instances, with this caution; none where the offender used a position of privilege, power or career to offend, unless explained; record any such weight as an assumption.

title: Extra-curial punishment: the custody-framed Delzoppo test vs the broader uses and examples in 7.8.2
statement: 7.8.2 says that, for injury or loss to mitigate, the offender must argue it would “(a) add to the burden of the appellant’s imprisonment; and (b) constitute a form of extra-curial punishment” (Delzoppo). The same section says such injury or loss is generally taken into account and may bear on just punishment, the weight of remorse and general and specific deterrence, and its examples include losses that do not obviously add to the burden of imprisonment (forfeited police superannuation; a culpable driver whose own child died). The Manual does not say how limb (a) applies where the sentence is not imprisonment, or to losses that do not affect custody. Handling: for imprisonment apply both limbs; for non-custodial outcomes, or losses bearing only on just punishment or deterrence, give weight with this caution rather than failing it; illness caused by the offender’s reaction to the consequences of offending is never extra-curial punishment. For injuries an offender suffers in the course of offending (e.g. arson), 27.2.4.4 says whether they mitigate is “unsettled” and depends on the circumstances; its examples go both ways (fn 4129: “some punishment”; mitigation; a more onerous custody). Handling: show this caution and do not fail reasoning that gives, or refuses, weight to such injuries.

refs.q: Where an offender suffers an injury or loss in the course of, or as a direct consequence of, their offending, this is a matter that a sentencing court will generally take into account.

title: Imitation or unloaded weapons: the Manual records competing authority
statement: Legislation and most cases draw little or no distinction between an imitation and a real weapon, but some authority has found that using an imitation or unloaded weapon makes the offending less serious. The Manual does not choose. Handling: where the facts involve an imitation, replica or unloaded weapon, show both views, do not fail reasoning that adopts either, and widen the estimate band. For violent property offences, 27.2.2.3 takes a position: such weapons “plainly” carry less risk and so are less dangerous than the genuine article, but can still instil terror and serious emotional damage and are dangerous given the potential police response. Apply that chapter-specific statement to violent property offences, with this caution. For firearm offences, 33.2.1.3 says the same maximum for a prohibited person’s possession of an imitation firearm “suggests that imitation firearms are treated with the same severity”, yet sentences where both offences are charged suggest courts treat imitation firearms as less serious; and since victims may believe they could be shot, a firearm’s incapacity to fire may be of limited relevance in certain circumstances. Apply 33.2.1.3 to imitation firearm offences, with this caution.

refs.q: Legislation and most cases draw little or no distinction between the use of an imitation or a real weapon; however, some authority has found that using an imitation or unloaded weapon makes the offending less serious.

title: Loss repaid by third parties: “little or no weight” (5.2.8.2) vs mitigation “not removed but may be lessened” (6.3.4.2)
statement: 5.2.8.2 says loss recouped from a third party such as an indemnity fund or insurer carries little or no weight in mitigation if it merely shifts the loss; 6.3.4.2 says restitution made by third parties or by court order does not remove mitigation but may lessen it. The Manual does not reconcile them (one may concern insurance recoupment, the other restitution paid on the offender’s behalf). Handling: where repayment came from someone other than the offender, show both statements, treat the weight as uncertain and do not fail either approach.

refs.q: Where the loss is recouped by payment from a third party, such as a professional indemnity fund or personal insurer, that consideration may be relevant but will carry little or no weight in mitigation if it simply represents the shifting of loss from one sector of the community to another.

title: Verdins evidence: “normally” expert evidence vs “expert evidence is required”; inference without direct evidence
statement: The Manual says Verdins requires cogent evidence “normally in the form of expert evidence”, then that “expert evidence is required” but not determinative; it also allows a court, without direct evidence, to infer that prison is more burdensome for a prisoner with a severe mental health condition. Handling: without expert evidence, state the assumption and that expert evidence is normally needed; do not fail burden-of-imprisonment reasoning that relies on the inference for a severe condition shown by other evidence.

refs.q: There needs to be cogent evidence, normally in the form of expert evidence, establishing on the balance of the probabilities that the Verdins principles are enlivened.

refs.q: While expert evidence is required, it is not determinative, and it is ultimately for the court, not a psychiatrist or psychologist, to decide if and how the Verdins principles apply in a given case.

title: Provocation as a sentencing factor: confined in causing-injury cases (25.2.1), not so confined in homicide (22.2.5)
statement: In causing-injury cases provocation is limited to words or deeds by the victim that induce the offender to lose control and offend almost immediately (25.2.1); in homicide, as a sentencing factor, it is not limited by the common-law test for reducing murder to manslaughter (provocation causing the accused to lose control, and capable of causing an ordinary person to lose control), may be cumulative, and may count where the conduct was excessive (22.2.5). The Manual does not explain the difference. Handling: apply each statement to its own offence class; where both arise in one sentencing exercise, show a caution.

title: Parole offending: no s 16(3B) order where parole is not cancelled at sentence — but s 77(7A) deems cancellation at sentence
statement: 3.3.3 says that where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing, no s 16(3B) order (cumulation or concurrency) can be made without breaching s 5(2AA); it also says s 77(7A) deems parole cancelled at the time of sentencing whenever a prison sentence is imposed for an offence committed on parole. The Manual does not say when the “not cancelled” case arises once s 77(7A) operates, and 8.4.1 states the parole cumulation default without the cancellation condition. Handling: intake asks whether parole was cancelled before sentencing. Yes → the s 16(3B) default applies (exceptional circumstances to displace it). No → no s 16(3B) order; caution, not error. Unknown → unresolved.

title: General deterrence for charges that could have been dealt with in the Children’s Court: “unclear”
statement: The Manual says it is unclear whether general deterrence applies where charges that might have been dealt with in the Children’s Court are dealt with in a superior court, and that it is “likely” to apply where punishment beyond that available under the CYFA (or s 32(3)(b)) is necessary. 10.1.2.1 adds CNK v The Queen: a child in the Supreme Court because charged with attempted murder, acquitted of it and convicted of other uplifted offences, had to be sentenced on the remaining uplifted charges as if exclusively governed by the CYFA, and general deterrence was held not relevant when sentencing children; the Court later clarified that it applies (possibly ameliorated) where CYFA dispositions are inadequate and adult custody is necessary. The Manual does not reconcile CNK’s first holding with a higher court’s power to impose a sentence under the Act where CYFA dispositions are inadequate (flag.cyfa_disposition_power), nor either holding with the “unclear” of 4.2.1. Handling: if the offender could have been dealt with in the Children’s Court, any reliance on general deterrence → caution, stating whether punishment beyond the CYFA or s 32(3)(b) is considered necessary; for a child, heavy reliance on general deterrence without that finding (or a finding that adult custody is necessary) remains an error, because general deterrence has minimal relevance when sentencing a child (audit.youth_principles (4), audit.purposes_balance (1)). Where a child is before the higher court only because of a charge of which they were acquitted (CNK), a disposition outside the CYFA → caution (this flag; audit.youth_principles (8), on the fact intake.court records), never error on this ground.
